newsitem.title: USA: Limit new CRP enrollment to 14 Mln acres - US panel.
newsitem.headline: Limit new CRP enrollment to 14 Mln acres - US panel.

text.p: A House appropriations subcommittee voted Wednesday to limit the Agriculture Department to accepting no more than 14 million acres into the Conservation Reserve this year.
The figure was far smaller than the 19 million acres mentioned in department documents. There have been objections to any deferrals in enrollment into the reserve.
Subcommittee members voted 6-5 for the restriction on new enrollments, which became part of a supplemental appropriations bill. It now goes to the full committee for consideration.
Representative Jim Walsh, New York Republican, said USDA did not have the capacity to accept more than 14 million acres this year so the restriction would be meaningless.
"We have an opportunity for the rest of the country to get its ducks in a row," said Walsh, who proposed the cap.
USDA officials expressed astonishment at the proposal and declined comment until they could examine the language.

In advisory language, the subcommittee said a cap on enrollment this year would allow USDA time to better target its use of the reserve, which pays farmers to take fragile land out of production for 10 years. It also expressed concern that some parts of the country would be given short shrift because of a rule that limits how much USDA will pay in rental rates.

The reserve, created in 1985, would experience one of its greatest turnovers this year. Contracts on some 21 million acres expire in September and during a signup period last month, farmers offered 25.6 million acres for the reserve.
The American Farm Bureau Federation said it wanted to assess the subcommittee action and its likely impact on farmers before commenting.

Ken Cook, a leading environmental advocate, said the cap "seems kind of arbitrary" because USDA had yet to indicate how much land it would accept. USDA has said it has no acreage quota for this year and that it would try to get the maximum environmental benefit from land it accepted.
"How do we know he (Walsh) hasn't hurt his part of the country?" Cook asked.
Skeptics have said USDA erred by making too much land eligible for consideration for the reserve.
